items.stem: A shopper presses Submit twice on a form that sends `POST /enrollments`. Before you try it: what will the table hold after two identical POST requests?

options.text: Two new rows, one for each request
options.feedback: POST is not idempotent. The server treats each POST as a new request and creates a new item every time, even when the body is identical.

options.text: One row, because the second request is identical to the first
options.feedback: The server does not compare requests. Each POST creates something new, so identical requests still produce duplicates.

options.text: One row, because the server rejects duplicates automatically
options.feedback: Servers reject duplicates only if you build that rule (for example a unique constraint or an idempotency key). Nothing in POST itself prevents them.

items.try: Select POST in the table above, type a course code, press Send, and then press Send the same one again. Count the rows.

items.stem: An edit form sends `PATCH /courses/ITENT45` with the body `{"units": 6}`. Because of network problems the same request reaches the server three times. What is the course's `units` value afterward?

options.text: 6, and the other fields are unchanged
options.feedback: PATCH sets the fields in the body to the given values. Repeating it writes the same value again, so PATCH here is idempotent.
PATCH with a plain value replaces the field. Only a request written as an increment, such as 'add 6 units', would add up, and that kind of request would not be idempotent.

options.text: 6, but the second and third requests create two extra courses
options.feedback: Creating new items is what POST does. PATCH changes an existing item and does not create anything.

options.text: The title and slots are cleared, because the body left them out
options.feedback: That describes PUT. PATCH leaves fields that are not in the body untouched.

items.stem: Select all that apply. Which of these statements about status codes are correct?

options.text: 401 means the server does not know who you are.
options.feedback: 401 is named Unauthorized, but it means unauthenticated. Sending login details and trying again can fix it.

options.text: 403 means the server knows who you are and still refuses.
options.feedback: Better credentials will not help, because the user is not allowed to do this.

options.text: 500 means the URL names nothing, so check the path and the id.
options.feedback: That describes 404. A 500 means the server code failed with an error while handling the request.

options.text: 404 means the server code raised an error while handling the request.
options.feedback: That describes 500. A 404 means the URL names nothing, so check the path and the id.

items.stem: A page needs 50 course titles and fetches them with 51 separate requests. Before you try it: if the browser uses HTTP/2, which number is still 51 times higher than for a single request?

options.text: The number of server handler runs
options.feedback: HTTP/2 sends the requests together over one connection, so the waiting drops. The server still runs its handler code, and does a database lookup, once per request.
HTTP/2 removes most of the waiting because it sends all the requests at once. The cost that remains is on the server.

options.text: Nothing. HTTP/2 makes 51 requests as cheap as one
options.feedback: HTTP/2 reduces the waiting. It does not reduce the work the server does for each request.

items.try: Set the first slider to 50, turn on HTTP/2, and compare the Server handler runs row with the Time spent waiting row.

items.stem: A catalog has 500 courses, and most students look at the first 10 before they leave. Which endpoint design suits this best?

options.text: `GET /courses?limit=20&offset=0`, then more pages as the student scrolls
options.feedback: Most of the 500 items are never seen, so loading one page at a time sends little data and shows the first screen quickly.

options.text: `GET /courses` returning all 500 courses in one response
options.feedback: This needs only one request, but it sends about 60 KB that most students never look at and makes the first screen wait for it.

options.text: `GET /courses/1`, `GET /courses/2` and so on, one request per course
options.feedback: This pays a round trip for every course and makes the server run its handler 500 times. A page of 20 items needs one request.
